note: Randomised trials at Microsoft and Accenture across 4,867 developers, 26 percent more completed tasks.
title: The Effects of Generative AI on High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Three Field Experiments with Software Developers
explain_beginner: This study asks a simple but important question: when software developers get access to an AI coding assistant that suggests code completions as they type, does it actually help them get more work done? Rather than relying on lab tests or surveys, the researchers worked with three real companies, Microsoft, Accenture, and an unnamed large firm, and ran controlled trials where some developers were given the AI tool and others were not, as part of normal day to day work. Combining results across all three companies, developers with the AI tool completed about a quarter more tasks than those without it. Interestingly, the biggest gains went to less experienced developers, who were also more likely to start using the tool in the first place. More seasoned developers saw smaller benefits. The results in any single company on its own were noisy and inconsistent, and only became clear once the three studies were combined, a reminder that real workplace effects can be harder to pin down than tidy lab results suggest.
explain_business: For a company weighing whether to roll out an AI coding assistant, this study is one of the more credible signals available, since it comes from real randomized trials inside operating businesses rather than lab settings or vendor demos. The headline number, a roughly 26 percent lift in completed tasks pooled across three companies, suggests a meaningful productivity return, but the authors are clear that any single company's own pilot may look muddled or inconclusive on its own, so leaders should expect noisy internal data and plan to measure over a longer period or larger group before judging results. The finding that junior and less experienced developers gained the most and adopted fastest has a direct staffing implication: these tools may pay off fastest by lifting newer team members toward senior level output, which matters for training budgets and hiring strategy. There is no evidence here about job displacement, code quality, or long run effects, so this remains a productivity and adoption finding rather than proof the technology changes headcount needs.
explain_practitioner: The authors report three randomized controlled trials run inside the ordinary business operations of Microsoft, Accenture, and an unnamed Fortune 100 company, covering 4,867 software developers total who were given or withheld access to an AI coding assistant that suggests code completions. The outcome measured was completed development tasks. Pooling the three experiments, the authors find a statistically significant 26.08 percent increase in completed tasks among developers using the tool, with a standard error of 10.3 percent. A key heterogeneity result is that less experienced developers adopted the tool at higher rates and captured larger productivity gains than more senior developers, suggesting the technology may narrow, rather than widen, skill based performance gaps within a team. The limitation the authors name directly is that each individual field experiment was noisy on its own, with results varying enough across sites that a clear effect only emerged once the three trials were pooled, meaning any single company's internal pilot could easily read as inconclusive despite a real underlying effect.
